summary: Describes Hierarchical Service Function Chaining, an experimental architecture that lets an organization split a large network into multiple administrative domains. The aim is to make large networks easier to design and control and to support independent functional groups.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of one giant factory line, you split it into smaller lines that each team runs, with a boss line linking them.

questions: how to scale service function chaining
subtitle: Hierarchical decomposition of large networks using service function chaining.

tldr.problem: Service Function Chaining (SFC) enables traffic-forwarding policies, but managing SFC across large, geographically dispersed networks is difficult because it requires a single control plane managing paths across millions of hosts and thousands of forwarding elements with potentially multiple operational teams.
tldr.mechanism: Hierarchical Service Function Chaining decomposes a large network into smaller subdomains, each managed by its own SFC control plane. Internal Boundary Nodes (IBNs) bridge between hierarchy levels, translating upper-level service paths into subdomain-specific paths while maintaining bidirectional symmetry and flow state.
tldr.outcome: Large networks become easier to design, control, and operate by separating concerns across administrative domains. Each team can manage their subdomain independently while the IBN ensures proper traffic flow across the hierarchy.

facts.label: Path config methods
facts.value: Five approaches (flow-stateful, metadata, unique paths, nested NSH, hybrid)

facts.label: Primary benefit
facts.value: Reduces upper-level path count from exponential to linear

today: RFC 8459 is an Experimental RFC published in September 2018. It provides guidance on implementing hierarchical service function chaining in large networks. The specification is open to experimentation and may be refined based on implementation experience.

sections.title: Hierarchical Service Function Chaining
sections.content:
Service Function Chaining (SFC) prescribes traffic-forwarding policies by directing packets through a chain of service functions. This works well in small, simple networks. However, managing a single SFC control plane across a large network with millions of hosts, thousands of forwarding elements, and multiple operational teams becomes extremely complex.

Hierarchical Service Function Chaining (hSFC) solves this by decomposing the network hierarchically into smaller SFC-enabled subdomains. A top-level domain manages overall traffic flows between subdomains, and each subdomain has its own control plane managing traffic within that subdomain. This decomposition makes large networks easier to design, simpler to control, and supportive of independent functional groups.

The hSFC architecture assumes strong trust relationships between domains (all under a single organization) and uses the Network Service Header (NSH) or similar labeling mechanisms to mark service function paths.
sections.plainLanguage: A big company has many departments. Instead of one boss controlling everyone's exact movements, the top boss decides which department a package visits, and each department's manager decides how the package moves inside their department.

sections.title: Upper and Lower Levels
sections.content:
hSFC creates a hierarchy with multiple levels. The upper level encompasses the entire network domain, managing classifiers and service function forwarders (SFFs) that distribute traffic across subdomains. The upper-level control plane configures coarse-grained traffic classification at network edges based on high-level criteria.

Each lower level is a subdomain with its own classifiers, SFFs, and service functions (SFs). At the ingress of a subdomain, packets are reclassified to select paths for service functions within that subdomain. At the egress, packets are returned to upper-level service paths.

The key benefit is that upper-level paths do not represent every combination of service functions in subdomains. Instead, upper-level SFPs specify which subdomains a packet should visit. Each subdomain then independently chooses the specific service functions to apply. This dramatically reduces the number of paths needed at the upper level compared to a flat, single-level SFC architecture.

The hierarchy can be applied recursively: a subdomain can itself contain further subdomains, allowing deep hierarchies in very large networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The top level is a map showing which cities (subdomains) a truck must visit. Each city has its own plan for where the truck goes inside the city. Cities don't care how other cities are organized.

sections.title: Internal Boundary Nodes (IBNs)
sections.content:
An Internal Boundary Node (IBN) is the crucial element that bridges upper and lower levels. To the upper level, an IBN acts like a regular service function. To the lower level, an IBN acts as both the entry and exit point (classifier and chain terminator).

When a packet arrives at an IBN from the upper level with an upper-level service path identifier (SPI) and service index (SI), the IBN must:

1) Receive the packet with upper-level SFC encapsulation

2) Extract the upper-level path information according to the configured method (saving it in state, metadata, or as a nested header)

3) Apply lower-level classification to select a subdomain-specific service path

4) Forward the packet along the subdomain path with lower-level encapsulation

5) At the chain termination, restore the upper-level SFC encapsulation using the saved information

6) Forward the packet back to the upper-level domain

This bridging function allows subdomains to be completely opaque to the upper level regarding their internal service functions.
sections.plainLanguage: An IBN is like a post office at the boundary between districts. It accepts packages marked with the city-level path, remembers what city they came from, marks them with the neighborhood path, routes them through the neighborhood, then restores the city-level marking when they leave.

sections.title: Path Configuration Methods
sections.content:
An IBN must preserve upper-level path information as packets transit the subdomain, then restore it when exiting. hSFC defines five approaches to this challenge:

Flow-Stateful: The IBN creates state indexed by transport-layer coordinates (5-tuple: source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, protocol). When a packet exits the subdomain, it looks up the state to restore the upper-level path. Limitation: cannot work with service functions that modify IP addresses (like NATs).

Metadata Encoding: The upper-level SPI and SI are pushed into a metadata field of the lower-level NSH header. When exiting, the metadata is retrieved to restore the upper-level path. Limitation: requires all service functions to properly forward metadata.

Unique Paths: Each upper-level path gets unique lower-level paths, so the lower-level SPI itself encodes which upper-level path to restore. Limitation: path count increases exponentially with hierarchy depth.

Nested NSH: The upper-level NSH header is placed inside the lower-level NSH header. The packet transits the subdomain with the outer NSH, preserving the inner NSH unchanged. At termination, the outer NSH is removed. Limitation: increases packet overhead and requires NSH-aware service functions.

Stateful-Metadata Hybrid: The IBN saves upper-level encapsulation indexed by a unique hSFC Flow ID placed in metadata. Works with NATs, different metadata schemes, and can restore all header information including TTL and flags.
sections.plainLanguage: There are five ways to remember an address when mail passes through a neighborhood: a ledger by who's mailing (flow state), a note inside the envelope (metadata), separate lanes for each address (unique paths), envelopes inside envelopes (nesting), or a ticket in the envelope (hybrid).

sections.title: Control Plane Organization
sections.content:
Each control-plane instance manages a single level of the hierarchy. The upper-level control plane configures top-level classifiers and manages end-to-end service chains across subdomains. Each subdomain control plane operates independently, configuring its own classifiers, service functions, and forwarding paths without visibility into other subdomains' policies.

This separation of concerns has important benefits:

  • Scalability: Each control plane only manages its domain's complexity
  • Independence: Subdomain changes do not affect the upper level
  • Bidirectional Symmetry: The subdomain classifier can ensure forward and reverse traffic paths traverse the same service function instances, critical for stateful services like firewalls and NATs
  • Load Balancing: Each subdomain can internally load-balance across multiple instances of the same service function, while the upper level sees it as a single logical service

hSFC also defines requirements for handling NSH-unaware service functions through IBN conversion, allowing hybrid NSH-aware and NSH-unaware domains to coexist.
sections.plainLanguage: The top boss only cares which cities must visit the package. Each city's mayor cares about local routes and which shops (service functions) handle each package. Neither interferes with the other.
